spans.assertion: paper title asserts referees give more red cards to darker-skinned players
paper title asserts the evidence for prejudice remains uncertain

spans.note: restates the research question of whether referees assign more red cards to darker-skinned players

spans.assertion: preliminary analyses were run to assess confounding or suppressor variables that might obscure the skin-tone/red-card association
player position and win-, draw-, and loss-percentages were identified as potential confounds
a multilevel regression was conducted predicting red cards from skin tone, the identified confounds, and games per dyad, with referee and referee country-of-origin as random intercepts
darker-skinned players received more red cards
the skin-tone/red-card association was not moderated by mean implicit or explicit prejudice in referees' countries-of-origin
treating red cards as a binomial event with multilevel logistic regression supported the same conclusions
darker-skinned players received fewer yellow cards
skin tone may predict whether severe fouls result in ejection (red card) rather than merely a caution (yellow card)
referees give more red cards and fewer yellow cards to darker-skinned players
this behavior is not associated with prejudice levels in the referees' country-of-origin
players with missing skin-tone ratings (N=467) were excluded from analyses involving the skin-tone variable
players missing skin-tone ratings were retained for all other analyses
the two separate coders' skin-tone ratings were averaged into a single index (M=0.29, SD=0.29)
players with missing position data (N=152) were assigned a value of 'unknown' so they could be retained in position analyses
a BMI variable (weight/height squared) was created to proxy how physically imposing a player is, as a potential predictor of red cards
BMI was selected as the best available proxy over height or weight alone, reasoning that among elite athletes higher BMI reflects muscularity rather than being overweight
a 'star status' variable was created as each player's average goals scored per game, as a proxy for fame that might lead to more lenient treatment
a 'game situation' variable was created based on the idea that losing teams may be more aggressive and draw more referee attention
match-level data was not available, so it was impossible to determine whether a player was winning or losing in the specific game in which they did or did not receive a red card
separate win, loss, and draw percentages were calculated for each player across all games in the data set as a proxy for game-situation frequency
no analyses were possible using club/league membership variables because each player was linked to only one 2012-2013 club while red-card data spanned multiple years
player age was not included in any analyses because a player's age at each particular match/referee pairing could not be determined

the analysis focused on whether skin tone could explain variation in red cards (an explanatory question) rather than how well it predicts red cards relative to other factors, and the first step was identifying variables that could serve as confounds or suppressors
variables were included as covariates only if correlated both with skin tone and with red cards received
variables correlated with red cards but not with skin tone were considered irrelevant and omitted from the final model

spans.note: clarifies the analysis is not designed to compare skin tone's predictive strength versus other factors, only whether any association exists

spans.assertion: multi-level modeling was used to account for the data's nested structure, citing Raudenbush & Bryk (2002)

spans.note: describes original nested data structure: players within player-referee dyads, referees within countries-of-origin

spans.assertion: the appropriate nesting structure for the regression model was evaluated empirically via a series of adjusted-means models regressing red cards on number of games per dyad
the necessary nesting level for the final model was determined by retaining any grouping variable that explained significant variance in red cards beyond the next simplest level
additional tests evaluated whether modeling the skin-tone slope as a random effect explained significantly more variance than modeling it as a fixed effect
differences between models were evaluated using χ2 tests on differences between -2 log likelihoods, citing Raudenbush & Bryk (2002)
individual referee (χ2(1)=70.10, p<.001) and referee country-of-origin (χ2(1)=100.70, p<.001) each explained significant variance in red cards beyond a model without them
nesting referee within referee country explained significant variance beyond either factor alone (χ2s(1)>29.10, ps<.001)
the three-level nesting structure (player within referee within referee country) was used in all subsequent reported analyses
modeling the skin-tone slope as a random effect did not explain additional variance beyond a fixed-effect model (χ2(4)=0.0001, p=1.0)
the skin-tone slope was therefore modeled as a fixed effect in all analyses
preliminary correlations were calculated among players' mean skin tone, physical stature, star status, and frequency of different game situations
a new player-level aggregated data matrix was constructed for this set of analyses
a one-way ANOVA was conducted to test whether players of different skin tones were equally distributed across positions
for variables significantly related to skin tone, follow-up analyses tested whether they also predicted red cards received
skin tone was not correlated with physical stature (r=.03, p=.32) or star status (r=.03, p=.27)

skin tone was correlated with game situation: darker-skinned players had lower win percentages (r=-.09, p=.001), higher draw percentages (r=.10, p<.001), and marginally higher loss percentages (r=.05, p=.06)
skin tone was not equally distributed across positions (F(12,1572)=5.42, p<.001)
a greater proportion of games won (β=-.06, p<.001) or drawn (β=-.04, p<.001) by a player with a particular referee was associated with fewer red cards
player position was differentially associated with the number of red cards received (F(12,142868)=11.92, p<.001)
win percentage, draw percentage, and position were used as covariates in all primary analyses, and loss percentage was also included since the three percentages are linearly dependent
the aggregated player-referee dyad structure was maintained, with number of games in each dyad included as a covariate to control for unequal pairing frequency
the researchers chose not to convert red cards to a proportion of games, because that would falsely equate different underlying game-count scenarios
the researchers initially chose not to analyze red cards as a binomial event, despite their rarity, believing it would not adequately account for varying player-referee pairing rates
Hypothesis 1 (whether skin tone was related to receiving a red card) was tested using a multilevel model of red cards per player-referee dyad

the model predicted red cards from fixed effects of mean skin tone, controlling for games in dyad, win/draw percentage, and alphabetically dummy-coded position, with dyads nested in referees nested in referee country, and random intercepts at each level
skin tone explained a small but significant amount of variance in red cards received (β=.008 [.003,.014], t(121627)=2.84, p=.005, d=0.02); darker-skinned players received slightly more red cards
Hypothesis 2a was tested by adding country-level implicit prejudice (IAT) and an IAT x skin-tone interaction term to the model
no evidence that country-level implicit prejudice (IAT) explained variation in the skin-tone/red-card association (β=.0003, t=0.12, p=.90, d=0.00)
Hypothesis 2b was tested by adding country-level explicit prejudice and an explicit-prejudice x skin-tone interaction term to the model
no evidence that country-level explicit prejudice explained variation in the skin-tone/red-card association (β=.0004, t=0.17, p=.87, d=0.00)
all primary analyses were repeated using yellow cards and a newly created total-bookings index (red + yellow + 2x yellow-red) as dependent variables
the same nesting structure and same covariates (position, win percentage, draw percentage, games per dyad) were supported for the yellow-card and total-bookings analyses
darker-skinned players received slightly fewer yellow cards than lighter-skinned players (β=-.005, t(121627)=2.06, p=.04, d=0.01)
the skin-tone/yellow-card association was not moderated by referee country-of-origin implicit or explicit prejudice
an alternate analysis recoded skin tone as a categorical contrast between African-appearing and non-African-appearing players, intended as a potentially more sensitive test of Hypotheses 2a/2b

visual inspection of coder ratings showed codes of .75/1.0 almost exclusively given to African-appearing players and 0/.25 almost exclusively to non-African-appearing players, while .50 ratings were mixed
players with mean skin-tone ratings below .50 were categorized as non-African appearing and those above .50 as African-appearing
players who scored exactly .50 (N=116) were dropped from this supplementary analysis
all primary analyses were repeated substituting the categorical African-appearance variable (-1/1) for mean skin-tone ratings
African-appearance did not significantly explain variance in red cards received (β=.014 [-.002,.030], t=1.73, p=.08, d=0.01)

African-appearance significantly explained variance in yellow cards (β=-.029, t=4.22, p<.001, d=0.03) and total bookings (β=-.022, t=3.24, p<.002, d=0.02), with African-appearing players receiving fewer of each
country-of-origin-level implicit prejudice (β=-.004, p=.54) and explicit prejudice (β=-.003, p=.64) did not moderate the number of red cards received
implicit prejudice did moderate the association between African-appearance and yellow cards (β=-.012, p<.04) and total bookings (β=-.012, p=.04)
follow-up analyses showed higher referee-country implicit prejudice was associated with fewer yellow cards and total bookings for African-appearing players
explicit prejudice did not moderate the number of yellow cards (β=-.008, p=.21) or total bookings (β=-.008, p=.17)
the distribution of red cards received is extremely non-normal, which could bias the analyses
as a robustness check, the primary hypothesis tests were repeated after converting red cards to a binomial variable within each dyad and using multilevel logistic regression with the same covariates
the binomial/logistic analysis supported the same conclusions: skin tone significantly explained variance in the likelihood of a red card (β=.275 [.09,.46], z=2.99, p=.003, OR=1.32 [1.09,1.58])
this association was not moderated by referee country-of-origin-level implicit prejudice (β=.484, z=0.14, p=.89, OR=1.62 [0.001,1224])
this association was not moderated by referee country-of-origin-level explicit prejudice (B=.39, z=0.81, p=.42, OR=1.48 [0.57,3.86])

overall results showed an extremely small but statistically robust association between skin tone and red cards given, independent of confounds involving physical stature, position, goal-scoring, and win/loss likelihood
darker-skinned players received more red cards

no evidence that referees from countries with higher implicit or explicit prejudice were more likely to assign red cards to darker-skinned players, indicating no direct link between the skin-tone effect and prejudice in this data

spans.note: notes country-level prejudice scores are a crude proxy for referees' individual prejudice, so absence of evidence does not permit conclusions about referees' decisions

spans.assertion: darker-skinned players received more red cards but fewer yellow cards, and there was no connection between skin tone and total bookings
speculates skin tone may not affect whether a foul is deemed booking-worthy at all, but may influence whether a severe foul results in a red card versus a yellow card
other possible confounds, such as clubs having a more aggressive playing style and possibly more darker-skinned players, could not be adequately assessed in this data set

spans.note: cautions that without controls for these confounds and direct evidence of prejudice, conclusions of referee attitudinal bias would be premature
